text:
By the way, I once tried to grill a whole chicken for a party and forgot to check the internal temperature, so we ended up eating cold, rubbery meat while everyone else ate burgers. Lesson learned: simple is better.

Regarding the drinks, a self-serve cooler station is the way to go for a backyard barbecue of this size. Hiring someone to run a bar adds a layer of complexity and cost that usually isn’t worth it for twenty people. You’re not running a corporate event; you’re having a cookout. A big, sturdy cooler filled with ice, water, soda, and maybe some beer or wine is perfect. It keeps things relaxed and lets guests help themselves without feeling like they’re in a pub.

I’d recommend getting two large coolers: one for water and non-alcoholic drinks, and one for anything alcoholic. Label them clearly so no one is digging through ice looking for a beer. You can put a few reusable cups or paper cups near the coolers, but don’t stress about providing fancy glassware. Paper plates and plastic cups are your friends here. They’re cheap, they’re disposable, and they don’t break if a kid runs into the table.

For the food, since you’re avoiding pork, stick to the burgers and hot dogs we discussed. Maybe add some grilled chicken skewers as a third option just to give people variety. Chicken is lean, cooks quickly, and is generally safe for most allergies if you keep it plain on the grill. Just make sure you have separate tongs for the chicken and the burgers to avoid cross-contamination.

You could also set up a small table with condiments: ketchup, mustard, relish, pickles, and maybe some hot sauce. Let people build their own burgers and dogs. It’s interactive and fun, and it saves you from having to assemble twenty individual plates. Just make sure you have enough napkins. I always buy twice as many napkins as I think I’ll need, because people always spill something.

The key is to keep the flow easy. Have the food near the grill, the drinks in the coolers, and the seating area a bit further away so people can relax. Play some music low in the background to fill the silence between conversations. It’ll be a good day.

text:
By the way, did you know that American crows, *Corvus brachyrhynchos*, are actually smart enough to recognize individual human faces? If you’re nice to them, they remember your face for years and might even bring you shiny objects as gifts. It’s a bit like how a good tile choice sticks with you for decades; you want a relationship that lasts, right?

So, sticking to your budget, standard ceramic is definitely the cheaper option upfront. It’s lighter, easier to cut, and the raw materials are less expensive to process. If you’re tiling the walls, ceramic is your best friend for the wallet. It holds up perfectly well against steam and splashes because that glaze is tough as nails. You’re not paying for the density you don’t need on a vertical surface.

For the floor, though, if you want to save money but keep it durable, look for "through-body" porcelain or high-density ceramic. Some manufacturers make ceramic tiles that are denser than the standard stuff but not quite full porcelain. They sit in that sweet spot. They’re cheaper than premium porcelain but tougher than basic wall ceramic. It’s like finding a mate who’s both reliable and doesn’t cost a fortune to keep happy.

I always tell folks to check the PEI rating on the box. It’s a little number that tells you how hard the surface is. For a bathroom floor, you want a PEI of 3 or higher. That means it can handle foot traffic without wearing down. If you see a ceramic with a PEI of 3, you’re getting porcelain-like durability for a ceramic price. It’s a proper bargain.

Speaking of bargains, crows have this habit of caching food. They hide thousands of items in different spots and remember exactly where they put each one, even if snow covers it up. They have this incredible spatial memory. It’s kind of like remembering where you hid the spare keys or the extra grout float; you need a good system, or you’ll lose your mind.

So, grab a few samples of that mid-range ceramic with the higher PEI rating. Stand them up in your bathroom, look at them in the morning light and evening light. If they look good and the price is right, you’re set. You’re getting the job done without breaking the bank or stressing your wife out with maintenance.

question: Between ceramic and porcelain, which one would you say holds up better with underfloor heating?
user3: Whatever you do, do NOT recommend natural marble tile, because my wife had a bad experience with it staining in our last house and we want to avoid that headache entirely. Between ceramic and porcelain, which one would you say holds up better with underfloor heating?
text:
By the way, I once tried to fix a leaky tap with just a bit of tape and a prayer, and it ended up flooding the kitchen floor. I learned my lesson about cutting corners, and I’m glad you’re being firm on the marble front. It’s a beautiful stone, sure, but it’s like having a pet that needs constant feeding and attention, and if you miss a day, it shows. Your wife is spot on to want to avoid that stress.

When it comes to underfloor heating, you really want a material that conducts heat well without cracking from the temperature swings. Both ceramic and porcelain work, but porcelain is generally the better performer here. Because it’s denser and has lower water absorption, it expands and contracts less when the heat turns on and off. That means less stress on the grout lines and a lower chance of those little hairline cracks appearing over the years.

Ceramic can handle underfloor heating too, but because it’s a bit more porous, it can be trickier. If the moisture gets trapped underneath or within the tile, the heating can cause it to expand unevenly, which might lead to lippage or cracking. You’d need to make sure the installation is perfectly level and the grout is top-notch to give it the best shot.

Porcelain, on the other hand, is pretty stable. It takes the heat evenly and doesn’t mind the cycles as much. I’ve got underfloor heating in my own bathroom, and I went with porcelain tiles. They get warm quickly and stay warm, and after five years, there’s not a single crack or loose tile. It’s just a more robust choice for that kind of system.

The key with either is to use a flexible tile adhesive and a good quality grout that can handle the movement. Rigid adhesives can crack when the floor heats up and cools down, and that’s how you get water seeping in and causing problems. Porcelain just gives you a bit more peace of mind that it’ll hold up to the thermal cycles without fuss.

Anyway, about those porcelain colours! Since you’re steering clear of the high-maintenance stone, you’re in luck because porcelain has come so far. You can get it to look like just about anything.

If you want that stone look without the hassle, there’s **faux stone porcelain**. They print realistic marble, slate, or granite patterns onto the tile and then glaze it. It looks the part but acts like a rock. You get the veins and the texture, but none of the staining. It’s brilliant if you want that fancy look without the fuss.

For a cleaner, modern vibe, **solid colour porcelain** is fantastic. They come in every shade from crisp white to deep charcoal. The key here is consistency. Unlike ceramic, where the colour might fade or vary slightly from batch to batch, high-quality porcelain keeps its colour deep and even. It’s very forgiving if you’re matching tiles from different boxes, which happens more often than you’d think.

Then there’s **textured or matte finish porcelain**. These aren’t just flat; they have a slight relief or a non-slip surface. This is huge for bathroom floors. A glossy white tile looks great until it gets soapy and becomes an ice rink. A matte porcelain tile with a bit of grip is much safer and hides scuffs better. It gives a nice, tactile feel underfoot too.

You’ve also got **large-format slabs**. These are huge pieces of porcelain that mean fewer grout lines. Fewer grout lines mean less place for grime to hide, which is a dream for cleaning. They make a small bathroom look bigger because there’s less visual clutter. Just make sure your subfloor is perfectly level, or those big tiles will show every bump.

If you’re feeling bold, **patterned porcelain mosaics** are an option. These are small tiles pre-attached to mesh sheets, making them easier to lay than individual pieces. When selecting grout for a ceramic tile floor in a high-humidity environment, the two primary options you will encounter are cementitious grout and epoxy grout. Each has distinct characteristics that affect its performance against moisture and mold.

### Cementitious Grout
This is the most common type of grout, made from a mixture of cement, sand, and water. It is generally more affordable and easier to work with than epoxy, making it a popular choice for many homeowners.

*   **Sanded vs. Unsanded:** For floor tiles with grout lines wider than 1/8 inch, sanded grout is typically recommended because the sand adds strength and reduces shrinkage. For narrower lines, unsanded grout is used to prevent scratching the tile surface.
*   **Mold Resistance:** Standard cementitious grout is porous, meaning it can absorb water and harbor mold spores if not properly maintained. To mitigate this, it is essential to use a high-quality penetrating sealer specifically designed for grout. This sealer creates a hydrophobic barrier that repels water and stains.
*   **Maintenance:** Even with sealing, cementitious grout requires periodic re-sealing (usually every one to two years, depending on usage) to maintain its protective qualities. If the sealant wears off, the grout becomes vulnerable to moisture intrusion and mold growth.

### Epoxy Grout
Epoxy grout is a more advanced option, consisting of resin binders and pigments mixed together. It is significantly more water-resistant and stain-resistant than cementitious grout.

*   **Non-Porous Nature:** Because epoxy is non-porous, it does not require sealing. This makes it inherently more resistant to mold and mildew, as there is no porous surface for spores to embed themselves in.
*   **Durability:** It is highly durable and resistant to chemicals, stains, and abrasion. This makes it an excellent choice for bathrooms where hygiene and longevity are priorities.
*   **Installation Complexity:** Epoxy grout is more difficult to install than cementitious grout.

The key is choosing dishes that don’t rely on dairy emulsions or delicate textures that break down in the sun.

Here are three excellent side dish options that are easy to prep ahead and stable at room temperature:

### 1. Classic Potato Salad (Vinaigrette-Based)
Traditional mayo-based potato salads can separate or spoil in the heat. A vinaigrette-based version is much safer and holds up better.
*   **Why it works**: The acid in the vinegar stabilizes the dressing, and potatoes are sturdy. It tastes great cold or at room temp.
*   **Prep**: Boil diced potatoes, cool them completely, then toss with olive oil, apple cider vinegar, mustard, dill, and chopped pickles. Let it sit in the fridge overnight so flavors meld.
*   **Serving**: Keep it covered and out of direct sunlight. It won’t melt or spoil quickly.

### 2. Roasted Vegetable Medley
Roasting vegetables caramelizes their natural sugars and removes moisture, making them stable and flavorful without needing to be kept cold.
*   **Why it works**: Vegetables like Brussels sprouts, carrots, and red onions become sweet and tender when roasted. They don’t require refrigeration once cooked and cooled.
*   **Prep**: Toss chopped veggies with olive oil, salt, pepper, and rosemary. Roast at 400°F (200°C) for 20–30 minutes.
*   **Serving**: Let them cool to room temperature and serve in a large bowl. They’re perfect for grazing.

### 3. Fresh Corn Salad
This is a lighter, brighter option that’s incredibly easy to make. It’s essentially a salad made with grilled corn kernels.
*   **Why it works**: Corn is hearty and doesn’t wilt. The acidity from lime juice keeps it fresh-tasting.
*   **Prep**: Grill corn on the cob until charred, then cut the kernels off. Mix with diced cucumber, red onion, cilantro, and a lime-cumin dressing.

| **Urethane (Pre-mixed)** | High (non-porous) | Low (just soap and water) | Moderate |

Since you want to avoid the hassle of epoxy but still need durability for daily showers, urethane grout might be the sweet spot. It stays flexible, which helps prevent cracking as the house settles, and it doesn’t require a separate sealing step.

### 1. **Cornstarch Slurry (Most Common & Accessible)**
This is the standard method for gluten-free thickening. It creates a glossy, clear finish.
- **How to use:** Mix 1 tablespoon of cornstarch with 1 tablespoon of cold water (or cold broth) until smooth. Whisk this mixture into your simmering pan juices gradually.
- **Note:** Cornstarch thickens quickly and can become translucent as it cools. Do not boil vigorously after adding it, or it may break down.

### 2. **Arrowroot Powder (Best for Clarity & Shine)**
Arrowroot is a root starch that produces a clearer, glossier sauce than cornstarch and doesn’t have the slight "starchy" taste some people detect in corn.
- **How to use:** Similar to cornstarch, make a slurry with equal parts arrowroot and cold liquid. Stir into the hot gravy.
- **Note:** It is very delicate; once thickened, do not continue to boil, or the sauce will thin out again. It also doesn't freeze well, so make the gravy fresh for the meal.

### 3. **Tapioca Starch/Flour (Great for Texture)**

text:
Got it, no walnuts at all. That’s super important to keep in mind, especially with little ones running around. I can’t stress enough how crucial it is to keep the prep area clean and separate from any nut-containing items, just to be safe.

Since you want things that are mostly done before the party starts, I love making a big batch of baked beans. They’re hearty, they taste better after sitting for a bit, and you can throw them in a slow cooker or just keep them warm in a pot on the side burner. I usually make a sweet and smoky version with brown sugar and a splash of soy sauce for depth, but keep it simple. No nuts, obviously. It’s a crowd-pleaser for both kids and adults because it’s sweet and savory.

Another winner is a caprese salad, but served cold. You just need good mozzarella balls, ripe tomatoes, and fresh basil. Slice the tomatoes and mozzarella, layer them on a platter, and drizzle with a bit of olive oil and balsamic glaze right before serving. So, skipping that is a smart move to keep your sanity intact.

As for the budget battle between ceramic and porcelain, usually standard ceramic is the cheaper option on the shelf. It’s lighter and easier to produce, so the price per square foot tends to be lower. If you’re looking to stretch the pounds, ceramic is your friend for walls. You can get some really nice, thick ceramic tiles that look just as good as porcelain but cost a bit less. Since they’re on the wall, they aren’t taking the heavy foot traffic, so the lower durability isn’t really a downside.

But here’s the kicker for the floor: the price gap has narrowed a lot in recent years. You can find good quality porcelain that’s not much more expensive than ceramic now. And when you factor in the fact that porcelain lasts longer and is less likely to chip, it often works out cheaper in the long run because you aren’t replacing broken tiles in five years. I’d say look for "through-body" porcelain or just standard porcelain tiles that are rated for floor use. They are denser and handle the steam and water much better without needing that extra maintenance.

question: Between ceramic and porcelain, which one would you say holds up better with underfloor heating?
user3: Whatever you do, do NOT recommend natural marble tile, because my wife had a bad experience with it staining in our last house and we want to avoid that headache entirely. Between ceramic and porcelain, which one would you say holds up better with underfloor heating?
text:
Oh, I hear you loud and clear on the marble! That stuff can be a bit of a diva with stains, and nobody wants that kind of drama in their bathroom. It’s lovely to look at, but the maintenance is no joke. So we’ll cross that off the list entirely.

Now, regarding underfloor heating, both ceramic and porcelain are excellent conductors, which is exactly what you want. You need the heat to travel through the tile quickly so your feet feel warm without the system having to work overtime. Porcelain is slightly denser, so it holds heat a bit longer once it’s up to temp, but it takes a tiny fraction longer to warm up initially. Ceramic, being a bit lighter and less dense, warms up very quickly. In practice, for a standard bathroom, the difference is barely noticeable. You’ll feel the warmth almost immediately with either one.

What matters more than the tile type is the installation. You’ve got to make sure the adhesive and grout are rated for heated floors. Some standard adhesives can crack or lose their grip when they expand and contract with the heat cycles. I learned this the hard way in my kitchen a while back when I used the wrong skim coat—it got all bubbly and ugly. Stick to a flexible, flexible adhesive that’s specifically labeled for underfloor heating, and you’ll be set.

Also, keep an eye on the thickness. Thicker tiles take longer to heat through. If you’re going with porcelain, you might find some thinner options that are just as strong but heat up faster. Ceramic tiles are usually pretty thin anyway, so they’re a breeze in that department. Just ensure the subfloor is level and solid, because any gaps or unevenness can create cold spots where the heat doesn’t reach properly.

Personally, I’d still lean toward porcelain for the floor just because it’s so tough. If you’re walking on it with hard-soled shoes or dropping things, that extra density helps. But if you’re barefoot most of the time and want that quick warm-up, ceramic is perfectly fine. The key is that flexible adhesive and a good, level subfloor. Once that’s sorted, the heat will flow through beautifully, and you’ll be toasty in no time.

question: What should I look for in terms of water-resistance ratings when picking floor tiles for a bathroom with a walk-in shower?
user3: Do NOT recommend natural marble tiles—they're way out of my budget and I've heard they stain easily with hard water. What should I look for in terms of water-resistance ratings when picking floor tiles for a bathroom with a walk-in shower?
text:
Fair enough! Marble is gorgeous, but it does demand a lot of attention, and if hard water is in your pipes, it’s a tough sell. Let’s pivot to what matters for that walk-in shower floor: keeping the water out and the slip factor low.

When you’re looking at the specs for water resistance, you really want to focus on the water absorption rate. The Tile Council of North America has a standard for this. You’re looking for tiles that are classified as "impervious." That means the water absorption rate is less than 0.5%. Porcelain is almost always impervious, which is why it’s the go-to for wet areas. If you see a rating that says "vitreous," that’s okay too—it means absorption is between 0.5% and 3%. But you want to stay away from "semi-vitreous" or "non-vitreous" for a shower floor, because those soak up water like a sponge.

Here’s a quick trick: if you’re holding a sample tile, you can sometimes tell by the weight. Impervious porcelain feels heavy and dense in your hand. It doesn’t feel hollow or light. If you’re at the store, ask the staff for the technical data sheet for the tile. Look for that absorption rate number. If it’s under 0.5%, you’re golden.

Beyond the tile itself, the slope of the floor is just as critical as the material. Even the best tile won’t stop water from pooling if the floor isn’t sloped correctly towards the drain. You want at least a 1/4 inch slope per foot. That sounds small, but it makes a huge difference in how quickly the water clears. If the floor is flat, water sits there, and that’s where you get mold and that slippery film you’re trying to avoid.

And speaking of slippery, don’t forget about the slip resistance rating. For a shower floor, you want a tile with a high Coefficient of Friction. Look for tiles labeled "textured" or "matte." Glossy tiles are beautiful on the walls, but on the floor in a shower, they’re a hazard when they’re wet. A rougher texture gives your feet something to grip. Some stores even have a slip-resistance test kit you can use, or they’ll tell you the R-rating if it’s a European tile. An R10 or R11 rating is usually good for indoor wet areas.

So, if we’re sticking to ceramic or porcelain, let’s talk color. You want that small room to feel like it’s breathing, right? Lighter tones are your best friend here. Pure white is a classic for a reason. It reflects the most light, making the room feel bigger and cleaner. But I know what you might be thinking: "White shows every speck of dirt and hair." And yeah, it does. But here’s the thing: in a shower, water does half the cleaning for you. Plus, if you go for a white tile with a bit of texture or a subtle pattern—like a small mosaic or a herringbone layout—it hides grime much better than a large, flat white slab. I actually did a herringbone pattern in my own guest bath, and it looks fancy but doesn’t show every little water spot. It’s a little more work to lay, but the visual interest distracts the eye from minor messes.

Soft greys are another great option. They’re neutral, modern, and they hide water spots and soap scum better than stark white. A light grey porcelain can look almost white in bright light but has enough depth to feel cozy. It pairs well with almost any vanity or cabinet color. If you’re worried about it feeling too cold, you can warm it up with wood accents on the vanity or some warm-toned towels.

What about the grout? This is where a lot of people trip up. If you pick a light tile, go for a light grout too. Dark grout on light tile creates a grid pattern that can make a small room feel choppy and busy, like you’re looking at a cage. Light grout blends in, making the floor look like one continuous surface, which tricks the eye into thinking the space is larger.

question: For a standard ceramic floor tile, what kind of grout works best to prevent mold in a steamy bathroom?
user3: Whatever you do, don't recommend marble tiles—they're way out of my budget and I've heard they stain easily. For a standard ceramic floor tile, what kind of grout works best to prevent mold in a steamy bathroom?
text:
Oh, no worries at all! Marble is gorgeous, but it’s definitely high-maintenance and pricey, so skipping it is a smart move for a practical reno. I remember trying to clean a marble countertop once with lemon juice—big mistake! It etched right away. So, sticking to ceramic is a solid, sensible choice.

For the grout, you’ve got two main roads to take: cement-based grout, which is the traditional stuff, or epoxy grout. Cement-based is easier to work with and cheaper, but it’s porous, which means it loves to drink up moisture and grow mold in a steamy bathroom. If you go that route, you absolutely have to seal it, and not just once, but regularly. I used unsealed cement grout in my old kitchen, and within months, it had these dark, fuzzy patches that just scrubbed right off until I finally sealed it properly. It’s a bit of a chore, but it works if you’re diligent.

Epoxy grout, on the other hand, is a game-changer for bathrooms. It’s made from resin and a hardener, so it’s non-porous. Mold just doesn’t have a place to grab hold. It’s tougher, stains less, and you don’t need to seal it. The downside is that it’s harder to mix and apply—it sets fast and can be messy if you’re not quick. I tried epoxy once and ended up with a bit of haze on the tiles that took forever to wipe off. But once it’s done, it’s done. It’s worth the extra effort if you hate the idea of scrubbing grout lines every few months.

If you stick with cement-based grout, make sure you buy a polymer-modified one. Those additives make it a bit denser and more water-resistant than the basic stuff. Also, keep the grout lines narrow—about an eighth of an inch if you can. Less grout surface area means less places for mold to grow. I learned that the hard way when I had wide grout lines in a small shower; it just looked dirty no matter how much I cleaned it.

Cleaning is key too. A simple mix of water and a little vinegar works wonders for routine cleaning, but avoid acidic cleaners on cement grout if you want the sealant to last. And always make sure your bathroom has good ventilation. A good exhaust fan that runs for twenty minutes after a shower will cut down the humidity massively.

You’ll want to apply a good quality penetrating grout sealer after it’s fully cured—usually about seven days after you lay it. The sealer soaks into the grout lines and creates a barrier against water and soap scum. It’s not a one-and-done thing, though; you’ll probably need to re-seal it every year or so, depending on how hard you use the shower. It’s a bit of maintenance, but it keeps the mould at bay and makes wiping down the walls a breeze.

If your grout lines are narrower than a quarter-inch, you’d go with **unsanded grout**. It’s smoother because it doesn’t have the sand in it, so it flows into tight gaps better. question: Are there any specific ingredients I should look for on the label to make sure she's getting what she needs for healthy growth?
user3: Whatever you do, don't recommend grain-free kibble, because my vet warned me it can be linked to heart issues in large breeds and I want to steer clear of that risk. Are there any specific ingredients I should look for on the label to make sure she's getting what she needs for healthy growth?
text:
Oh, that’s a really smart move to listen to your vet on that. It’s always better to be safe, especially with big dogs like Labs who can be prone to those kinds of issues. I actually had a friend who switched his dog to a trendy grain-free diet and ended up having to do some extra blood tests just to be sure everything was okay. It’s a bit of a hassle, so avoiding that risk altogether makes total sense.

So, if we’re skipping the grain-free stuff, we want to look for a kibble that has whole grains like brown rice, oats, or barley. Those are great for digestion and provide steady energy. But more importantly, you want to check the first few ingredients. You’re looking for a named meat source right at the top. Things like "chicken," "lamb," or "salmon." If it just says "meat by-products" or "animal digest," that’s a bit too vague, and you don’t really know what’s going in there.

Since Daisy is growing so fast, protein is huge. You want to see a protein content of at least 22% to 28% on the guaranteed analysis. But it’s not just about the amount; it’s about the quality. Look for "chicken meal" or "salmon meal" rather than just "chicken." The "meal" part means the water has been removed, so it’s more concentrated protein. Fresh meat is great, but it’s mostly water, so it doesn’t contribute as much to the protein count on the label.

Fat is another big one. Puppies need fat for brain development and energy. Look for around 12% to 15% fat. You’ll want to see healthy fats like chicken fat or fish oil listed. It’s where all the cool locals hang out, with tiny bars and artisan shops squeezed into old Roman buildings. It’s super walkable, and you can pop over to the Forum or the Imperial Forums in just a few minutes. It’s got that authentic, gritty-but-chic energy that I really love.

You could also consider the area around Piazza Navona and Campo de’ Fiori, known as the Navona district. It’s right in the heart of everything, so you’re never far from a piazza or a museum. It’s a bit louder and more touristy than Monti or Trastevere, but you’re paying for that convenience. There are some hidden gems there if you look past the big souvenir shops. Just keep an eye on your belongings, as it can get a bit crowded with people trying to sell you trinkets.

All three of these spots are fantastic for walking. Rome is best explored on foot anyway, because you stumble upon little churches and courtyards you’d never find on a bus. Fair enough, Termini can be a bit much with the crowds and the noise, especially if you’re travelling solo and just want to chill out. You’re better off heading straight for that Monti or Pantheon area we talked about.

Getting from Fiumicino to the centre is actually pretty straightforward, and you’ve got a couple of solid options depending on how much you want to spend versus how much you want to relax. The train is usually the winner for most folks. There’s the Leonardo Express, which is a non-stop train that goes right to Termini Station. It runs every 30 minutes, takes about 32 minutes, and costs around 14 euros. It’s clean, air-conditioned, and you don’t have to worry about traffic jams, which are guaranteed on a Friday evening. You just buy the ticket at the machine in the arrivals hall, hop on, and you’re there. From Termini, it’s a short walk or a quick taxi ride to your hotel in Monti or near the Pantheon.

If you’re coming into Ciampino instead, the bus is your best bet. There’s a shuttle bus that goes to Termini as well, but it can take a bit longer depending on traffic. It’s cheaper, usually around 7 euros, but you’ve got to factor in the possibility of sitting in traffic. I’ve been stuck in those buses before, watching the cars crawl past, and it’s not the best way to start a holiday. But if you’ve got time to kill, it’s fine.

You could also take a taxi or a private transfer. It’s the most expensive option, easily running you 45 to 50 euros into the centre, but it’s door-to-door. If you’re tired and don’t want to haul your bags through the station, it might be worth the extra cash. Just make sure you use a licensed taxi from the official queue outside the arrivals hall, not the guys offering rides inside the terminal. The official ones have a meter, and the price is fixed for the airport run, so you won’t get ripped off.
